summary: Global disruption conditions have deteriorated materially as the U.S.-Iran war is constricting Hormuz traffic, pushing oil above $100 per barrel, threatening Red Sea alternatives, and feeding inflation and bond-market stress. Civilian disruption is still uneven rather than systemic, but the fastest credible deterioration pathway is now measured in days to weeks through fuel, shipping, price, and financial channels.
primary_driver: Escalating Middle East conflict is coupling maritime chokepoint disruption with an energy-price shock, inflation pressure, trade friction, and tightening financial conditions.
primary_stabilizers: Global financial markets, payment systems, and major exchanges remain operational despite higher oil prices, falling equities, and rising bond yields.
Alternative maritime routes remain partially functional: approximately 28 commodity vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb on September 9, near its recent average.

Existing oil inventories and emergency-stock mechanisms provide some buffer against an immediate total supply failure, even though spare capacity and reserve protection are less comfortable than earlier in the conflict.
Central banks and governments are actively responding to inflation and energy stress rather than allowing the shock to remain unmanaged.
The observed natural-disaster impacts remain geographically concentrated, with no indication of a simultaneous global weather or earthquake catastrophe.

domains.name: Energy security
domains.rationale: Attacks on tankers and regional energy infrastructure have pushed Brent above $100 per barrel while sharply reducing Hormuz traffic, creating an actively unfolding risk to oil, LNG, fuel prices, and electricity costs.

domains.name: Military / geopolitical
domains.rationale: The U.S.-Iran conflict has expanded into repeated attacks on ships, bases, and energy facilities, while Houthi forces have seized a strategic Yemeni port and increased the risk of a second maritime chokepoint crisis.

domains.name: Supply chain & transportation
domains.rationale: Hormuz commodity-vessel transits have fallen to single digits and Red Sea security is deteriorating, raising near-term risks to tanker capacity, rerouting, insurance, delivery times, and freight costs.

domains.name: Global trade fragmentation
domains.rationale: The U.S.-Canada dispute has escalated from tariffs to targeted import bans and retaliation, adding a major North American trade barrier to already-fragmented global commerce.

domains.name: Technology chokepoints
domains.rationale: Export controls and concentration in advanced semiconductor equipment and critical-mineral refining remain credible disruption pathways, but current reporting shows strategic vulnerability more clearly than immediate civilian shortages.

domains.name: Critical infrastructure / cyber
domains.rationale: Wartime cyber targeting of water, power, ports, telecom, and other infrastructure is a credible escalation vector, although broad cross-border outages or prolonged civilian service failures are not yet observed.

domains.name: Financial-system stress
domains.rationale: The oil shock is lifting inflation expectations and long-term bond yields, prompting central-bank tightening and increasing the risk of weaker credit, higher borrowing costs, and market stress.

domains.name: Food & agriculture
domains.rationale: Higher fuel, fertilizer, insurance, and freight costs are increasing food-system vulnerability, but broad global food shortages or rationing are not currently evident.

domains.name: Domestic institutional stress
domains.rationale: Emergency measures, wartime economic controls, trade retaliation, and political polarization could affect civilian access and prices, though widespread domestic institutional breakdown is not observed.

domains.name: Public health / biological
domains.rationale: Polio remains an international public-health emergency in affected regions, but there is no current evidence of a new pandemic-scale biological event producing broad global civilian disruption.

domains.name: Natural / environmental
domains.rationale: Hurricane Lowell has caused deaths, power outages, road damage, and loss of cargo-port functionality in Hawaii, demonstrating localized disruption but not a global natural-disaster cascade.

areas_to_watch.name: Hormuz traffic and LNG departures
areas_to_watch.why: A sustained period of near-zero tanker and LNG movement would convert a severe price shock into physical fuel shortages, rationing, and electricity stress in import-dependent regions.

areas_to_watch.name: Attacks on Saudi, UAE, Iraqi, or Iranian energy infrastructure
areas_to_watch.why: Additional damage to production, refining, export terminals, or pipelines could remove remaining market buffers and cause a second step-change in oil and fuel prices.

areas_to_watch.name: Bab el-Mandeb and Red Sea control
areas_to_watch.why: A simultaneous disruption of Hormuz and the Red Sea would sharply reduce viable energy and container routes and force longer, more expensive diversions.

areas_to_watch.name: Expansion of U.S.-Canada trade restrictions
areas_to_watch.why: Broader bans or retaliation involving energy, food, metals, automotive inputs, or agricultural equipment would create immediate North American price and availability effects.

areas_to_watch.name: Cyber incidents causing prolonged utility or telecom outages
areas_to_watch.why: A confirmed multi-state or cross-border outage affecting power, water, ports, payments, GPS, or communications would rapidly increase civilian disruption beyond current market effects.

areas_to_watch.name: Bond-market deterioration and credit-spread widening
areas_to_watch.why: Persistent oil-driven inflation combined with higher sovereign yields could tighten household, business, and government financing while amplifying supply-chain stress.

signals.title: Hormuz shipping traffic falls to single digits
signals.summary: Reuters reported that only seven commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on September 9, below the recent average, with no LNG carriers exiting. This is direct evidence of an active maritime and energy-flow disruption rather than a purely speculative threat.

signals.title: Oil remains above $100 as Middle East attacks intensify
signals.summary: Brent crude remained above $100 per barrel after attacks involving U.S. and Iranian forces and regional shipping. Higher oil prices are already transmitting into inflation expectations, transport costs, and household fuel exposure.

signals.title: Houthi forces seize strategic Yemeni port
signals.summary: The reported capture of a key Yemeni port raises the risk that the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb become materially less reliable as an alternative to disrupted Hormuz traffic. A two-chokepoint disruption would substantially increase global freight and energy risk.

signals.title: U.S.-Canada tariff dispute escalates to import bans
signals.summary: The United States has banned selected Canadian alcoholic beverages, motorcycles, and dairy products after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs. The move indicates that the trade conflict is shifting from tariff management toward direct product restrictions.

signals.title: Energy shock lifts global bond yields
signals.summary: Reuters reported that 10-year U.S. Treasury yields reached their highest level since 2023 as oil prices renewed inflation fears. The combination raises the risk of tighter credit and weaker economic activity even while financial plumbing remains functional.

signals.title: European Central Bank raises rates against energy inflation
signals.summary: The ECB raised interest rates to counter inflation fueled by the Iran war and higher energy prices. The action is a stabilizing response but also confirms that the shock is broad enough to affect monetary policy.

signals.title: Hurricane Lowell disrupts Hawaii infrastructure
signals.summary: The storm has caused deaths, power outages, road damage, and the loss of a cargo port serving food and fuel deliveries to Lanai. The event is geographically limited but demonstrates current localized civilian disruption from a natural hazard.

signals.title: Polio remains an international public-health emergency
signals.summary: WHO extended temporary recommendations because of continuing international spread risks involving wild and circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus. The situation warrants monitoring but is not currently classified as a pandemic emergency.

preparedness_actions: Complete previously planned purchases of essential household supplies without hoarding.
Top off normal prescriptions, fuel, water storage, and backup-power readiness where practical and lawful.
Keep additional payment options and emergency cash accessible.
Confirm family communications, transportation, and contingency plans.
Follow official emergency guidance for any affected region or infrastructure system.
historical_note: Illustrative reference markers only; not used in the live score until formal back-testing is completed.

methodology.note: All-hazards early-warning assessment, not a probability forecast or prediction that a specific disaster will occur.
methodology.formula: Leading Threat Pressure = mean of the four highest domain threat scores. Observed Civilian Disruption = mean of the four highest domain impact scores. Preparedness Urgency = 55% Leading Threat Pressure + 30% Observed Civilian Disruption + 15% Cross-System Coupling, rounded.
methodology.stage_guardrails: IMMINENT DISRUPTION requires both a high urgency score and material observed disruption. ACTIVE DISRUPTION requires broad, documented system impairment; threat scores alone cannot trigger it.
methodology.domains: Military/geopolitical, energy, trade, supply chain, technology, critical infrastructure/cyber, financial, food/agriculture, domestic institutional, public health, and natural/environmental.
